title: Principle 6: Feedback: Don't dodge the punches
hook: Comment panes are useful only while the draft can still change shape.
counterintuition: Feedback is not a vote on your worth, but a way to expose private errors while the work is still soft enough to change.
tryThisNow: Send one unfinished piece of work to the smallest qualified reviewer and ask for one correction tied to the target standard.
keyTakeaway: Expose work early enough for correction to matter, seek feedback from the right standard, and separate useful signals from noise without hiding from the punch.

breakdown.fastRead:
Claire keeps the grant draft open beside the deadline calendar. The sentences are rough, but the budget logic can still be fixed today. If she waits until the prose feels safe, the error will be polished into place.

She sends the draft and asks for comments on the budget argument only. Feedback works when correction can still alter the work. Protected errors become stronger each day they stay private.

Do not ask the world to admire the draft. Ask it to hit the part that can still be repaired.
breakdown.deepRead:
Chris pins two critique sheets above the studio desk. Different reviewers wrote the same note about the poster hierarchy. His first reaction is heat in the face, then a wish to dismiss both comments as taste.

Repetition is data.

Feedback is uncomfortable because it removes the private version of the work. The sketch, draft, route, recording, or report now has to answer back through another person. That sting is not the goal, but it often guards the door. If the work never meets correction, the learner keeps practicing the same hidden error.

Antoine posts three imperfect pottery photos against a gray backdrop. Buyers do not complain about glaze, as he expected. They ask about mug size and whether the chip is intentional. The response shows missing information, not personal failure. He changes the listing before making twenty more pieces.

Not every comment deserves obedience. Feedback should be judged by the task standard. A vague insult is noise. A repeated note tied to the target is signal. The skill is staying exposed long enough to tell the difference.

Claire keeps the request narrow because broad feedback often turns into taste. Budget logic is the risky part, so she asks for that. The comment pane becomes useful because it has a job: find the argument gap before the grant draft hardens into a polished mistake.
breakdown.fullRead:
Sofia unfolds the lab rubric beside a rack of labeled samples. Her partner offers to read the report for neatness. Sofia almost says yes because neatness feels safe. The grading standard says something sharper: uncertainty explanation.

"Can you mark only that section?" she asks.

The request makes the feedback narrower and more useful. Instead of inviting general opinion, she directs the reviewer toward the part the assignment will judge. That is the difference between exposure and flinching in every direction.

What correction would still change the next version?

Ask that before you seek feedback. Early correction has leverage. Late correction often becomes regret. A grant budget can be fixed before submission. A design hierarchy can be changed before printing. A solo recording can be adjusted before the performance. A route plan can be repaired before the next delivery window. Feedback loses power when pride delays it until the work is too finished to move.

Chidi hears the problem in a phone voice memo under a marked choral score. At 7:45 p.m., he predicts one more private run will smooth the breath timing. Instead, he sends the rough take to the conductor and asks for one correction on breath before the high phrase. The answer is small, pointed, and immediately useful.

There is a second discipline after exposure: filtering. Marta receives complaints about a delivery map with three late stops marked in orange. Some comments are venting. One correction appears in real delivery notes twice: the downtown route assumes a left turn that trucks cannot make at rush hour. In the postmortem, she keeps that correction and drops the rest.

Useful filtering is not defensiveness. Defensiveness starts with the wish to make the comment go away. Filtering starts with the standard and asks whether the comment helps the work meet it. That difference keeps Marta from obeying noise and keeps Claire from hiding from budget logic.

Feedback is not a command to obey every voice. It is a way to make errors visible while action is still possible. The learner who dodges all correction stays comfortable and blind. The learner who obeys every complaint becomes scattered. The useful path sits between those failures: seek the reviewer close to the standard, ask for the correction that matters now, and let the work absorb the hit.

Send the draft while it can still change. Then use the bruise as a map.

Repeated feedback deserves special treatment. One harsh comment can be mood, taste, or noise. Two independent readers naming the same blocked turn on Marta's route map is different. Repetition is data when separate readers find the same break in the work. That signal should move ahead of the comments that merely sting. Feedback is strongest when it is early enough to use and specific enough to sort.

examples.title: Claire Sends the Draft Before It Is Pretty

planSpec.domain: Claire, a grant writer sending an early draft while comments can still change it
planSpec.audience: a learner who has been mistaking motion for progress
planSpec.stakes: whether the next month produces visible evidence or another private feeling of effort
planSpec.requiredBeat: Claire sends the grant draft before polishing the language because the budget logic can still be corrected today.

examples.scenario: A shared-document comment pane sits open beside Claire's grant deadline calendar. The prose is still rough, and the budget logic is the part most likely to fail. Her finger pauses above Share. Waiting would make the draft prettier and less movable, so she sends it now with one request: mark the budget argument before noon. Claire's review slot is 9:16 a.m. Claire must decide to send the unfinished draft to the qualified reviewer and ask for budget-logic comments only.
examples.whatToDo: Send the unfinished draft to the qualified reviewer and ask for budget-logic comments only.
examples.whyItMatters: Feedback has leverage while the draft can change. Polishing first may protect the very error that needs correction.

examples.title: Chris Treats Repeated Critique as Data

planSpec.domain: Chris, a design student hearing the same critique from two reviewers
planSpec.audience: a practitioner under a near-term performance constraint
planSpec.stakes: whether a deadline exposes the weakness early enough to adjust
planSpec.requiredBeat: Chris writes down the design critique that two reviewers repeat and treats the repetition as data, not insult.

examples.scenario: You are beside Chris at the studio pinboard, where two critique sheets overlap under the same poster sketch. Both reviewers marked hierarchy. His jaw tightens because the poster felt finished last night. The next move is available: call the comments unfair, or write hierarchy in the margin and treat the repetition as evidence. Chris must decide to write down the repeated critique, revise the hierarchy first, and leave taste arguments until after the task-standard issue is fixed.
examples.whatToDo: Write down the repeated critique, revise the hierarchy first, and leave taste arguments until after the task-standard issue is fixed.
examples.whyItMatters: Two reviewers naming the same weakness is a signal. Treating it as insult keeps the error protected.

examples.title: Antoine Lets Buyers Find the Missing Detail

planSpec.domain: Antoine, a pottery seller posting imperfect product photos for real buyer response
planSpec.audience: a learner who has been mistaking motion for progress
planSpec.stakes: whether the learner keeps credibility with a reviewer, client, teacher, or team
planSpec.requiredBeat: Antoine posts three imperfect pottery photos and watches which buyer question exposes the missing information.

examples.scenario: The shop page shows a chipped mug photographed on a gray backdrop. Antoine wants another private photo session before anyone sees it. Instead, he posts three imperfect photos and watches the first buyer questions arrive. Size, handle feel, and chip detail matter more than the glaze caption he kept rewriting. Antoine's review slot is 12:33 p.m. Antoine must decide to post the limited set, read buyer questions, and revise the listing around the missing information they expose.
examples.whatToDo: Post the limited set, read buyer questions, and revise the listing around the missing information they expose.
examples.whyItMatters: Real buyer response finds the gaps Antoine cannot see alone. Private polish would only improve the wrong details.

examples.title: Sofia Asks for the Rubric Comment

planSpec.domain: Sofia, a lab assistant requesting comments tied to the grading standard
planSpec.audience: a practitioner under a near-term performance constraint
planSpec.stakes: whether the project survives contact with a real schedule and real standards
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sofia asks for lab comments only on the rubric dimension that will judge the assignment, not on general neatness.

examples.scenario: "Want me to clean up the wording?" Ruth asks, then catches herself and points to the rubric folded beside the sample rack. Sofia shakes her head. "Only mark uncertainty explanation," she says. The report is due tomorrow, and she chooses feedback tied to the grading standard instead of safer comments on neatness. Sofia must decide to ask for comments on the rubric dimension that will judge the report, not on general polish.
examples.whatToDo: Ask for comments on the rubric dimension that will judge the report, not on general polish.
examples.whyItMatters: Feedback should answer the standard. Neatness comments might feel easier, but they will not fix the section that controls the grade.

examples.title: Chidi Sends the Rough Breath Take

planSpec.domain: Chidi, a choir soloist recording a rough take for targeted correction
planSpec.audience: a learner who has been mistaking motion for progress
planSpec.stakes: whether comfort keeps protecting the exact skill gap that matters
planSpec.requiredBeat: Chidi records the rough choir solo and asks the conductor for one correction on breath timing.

examples.scenario: At 7:45 p.m., Chidi pauses a phone voice memo under a marked choral score. He predicts one more private run will make the breath timing safe. The high phrase fails again. He sends the rough take anyway and asks the conductor for one correction on breath before the phrase, not a general opinion on the solo. Chidi must decide to send the rough take and ask for one breath-timing correction tied to the failing phrase.
examples.whatToDo: Send the rough take and ask for one breath-timing correction tied to the failing phrase.
examples.whyItMatters: Private repetition keeps the same miss hidden. A narrow correction gives Chidi something he can change before rehearsal.

examples.title: Marta Keeps the Routing Correction

planSpec.domain: Marta, a logistics planner filtering noisy comments without hiding from precise ones
planSpec.audience: a practitioner under a near-term performance constraint
planSpec.stakes: whether the next attempt changes the skill instead of decorating the plan
planSpec.requiredBeat: Marta separates noisy logistics complaints from the one routing correction that keeps appearing in real deliveries.

examples.scenario: It took Marta one rough delivery day to sort the orange marks on the route map. Some comments were heat. Two drivers named the same blocked left turn. In the postmortem, she crosses out the noisy complaints, keeps the repeated routing correction, and rebuilds the downtown loop around that signal.
examples.whatToDo: Filter the comments by task standard and repetition, then fix the route around the precise correction that real deliveries confirmed.
examples.whyItMatters: Feedback is useful when it sharpens the work. Marta should not hide from complaints, but she should not obey noise either.

questions.prompt: A grant writer waits to request comments until the language is polished, but the budget logic may be wrong. What should she do? The next choice will decide whether today's work produces evidence or only another round of comfort.
choices: Send the rough draft now for budget-logic correction.
Polish first so the reviewer is impressed.
Ask for general encouragement before sharing details.
questions.explanation: Budget logic can still change now. Polishing first may preserve the error, and encouragement does not expose the weak part.

questions.prompt: Two design reviewers separately mark the same hierarchy problem. What is the best interpretation? A reviewer will see the result tomorrow, so the answer must choose an action rather than a preference.
choices: The reviewers are probably copying each other.
The repeated note is data tied to the task.
The student should ignore critique to protect originality.
questions.explanation: Repeated correction is a strong signal. Assuming bad faith or hiding behind originality protects the weakness.

questions.prompt: A pottery seller fears posting imperfect photos, but buyers keep asking about size when he finally posts. What did feedback reveal? The deadline is close enough that extra preparation would hide the weakness instead of testing it.
choices: His glaze style is wrong.
He should stop selling until photos are perfect.
The listing lacked information buyers needed.
questions.explanation: Buyer questions exposed missing information, not necessarily bad pottery. Waiting for perfect photos would have delayed that signal.

questions.prompt: A lab assistant asks for comments on neatness when the rubric grades uncertainty explanation. What should change? A real artifact is waiting on the table, and the learner needs a move that changes the next attempt.
choices: Ask for feedback on uncertainty explanation.
Ask for more comments from anyone available.
Avoid feedback because rubrics are enough.
questions.explanation: Feedback should match the task standard. General comments may be easier to hear but less useful for the grade.

questions.prompt: A soloist keeps recording private takes and never sends one to the conductor. Breath timing stays weak. What is the right feedback request? Limited time remains before review, so the best option should expose the skill gap quickly.
choices: Wait until the take is performance-ready.
Send a rough take and ask for one correction on breath timing.
Ask friends whether the solo sounds good overall.
questions.explanation: The rough take exposes the exact weakness while it can still be fixed. Waiting or asking general listeners dodges targeted correction.

questions.prompt: A logistics planner receives angry comments and one repeated route correction from drivers. What should she keep? Yesterday's visible miss is still on the page, so the response should use that evidence.
choices: Every complaint equally.
Only praise from managers.
The repeated correction tied to real delivery constraints.
questions.explanation: Useful feedback is tied to the task standard and repeated in the work. Noise should be filtered without hiding from the precise signal.

questions.prompt: A learner says feedback is valuable only when it feels encouraging. What correction fits best? The learner can protect the old habit or make the next attempt more honest under pressure.
choices: Feedback is valuable when it makes a fixable weakness visible.
Discouraging comments are always more honest.
All criticism should be followed immediately.
questions.explanation: The value is in useful correction, not emotional tone alone. Harshness is not proof, and not every criticism deserves obedience.

questions.prompt: A writer receives feedback after submission, when no changes are possible. What was lost? One session remains before feedback, and the answer should choose the useful constraint.
choices: The chance to feel confident beforehand.
The chance for correction to alter the work.
The need to filter noisy comments.
questions.explanation: Feedback has less leverage after the work cannot move. Confidence and filtering matter, but timing is the main failure.

questions.prompt: Two learners seek feedback. One asks everyone for general thoughts; the other asks a qualified reviewer for one standard-tied correction. Which is stronger?
choices: The general request, because more comments mean more learning.
Neither, because feedback should be avoided until mastery.
The qualified, narrow request, because it targets the work's judging standard.
questions.explanation: A narrow request to the right reviewer produces usable correction. More general comments can create noise, and delaying feedback protects errors.

reviewCards.back: When the work is exposed early enough that correction can still change the next version.

reviewCards.front: How should you choose what feedback to request?
reviewCards.back: Tie the request to the standard that will judge the work, not to general polish or comfort.

reviewCards.front: What should you do with repeated, standard-tied critique?
reviewCards.back: Treat it as signal. Repetition from qualified sources points to a weakness worth fixing.

reviewCards.front: Why is obeying every comment a mistake?
reviewCards.back: Some feedback is noise. Use the task standard and real-world repetition to separate useful correction from venting.
It protects errors from correction and lets the learner keep practicing a private, flawed version of the work.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is useful exposure. You show imperfect work to the smallest qualified reviewer, ask for correction tied to the target standard, and filter comments without hiding from the signal.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a draft can still change, then send it for one standard-tied correction before polishing.
If two reviewers repeat a critique, then treat the repetition as data and revise that element first.
If private runs keep failing, then send a rough recording and request one targeted correction.
If feedback is noisy, then keep comments repeated by real task conditions and drop the rest.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Send one unfinished piece of work to the smallest qualified reviewer and ask for one correction tied to the target standard.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, expose one unfinished artifact before it feels safe and write down which correction changed the next version.

memorableLines.why: It frames avoidance as active damage, not harmless delay.

memorableLines.text: Repetition is data when separate readers find the same break in the work.
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a clean rule for repeated critique.
